These features were standardised and averaged into a complexity index, following approaches used in affective image databases [53, 54]. On average, images were moderately dark (M = 0.28, SD = 0.10) with moderate-to-high contrast (M = 0.84, SD = 0.27, range = 0.20 -1.88). The Visual Complexity Index was expressed as a z-score (0 = mean complexity), ranging from -1.5 to +2.8 (SD = 0.61), indicating substantial variation in visual detail and color diversity across the image set.

Post-level characteristics

Each viewing episode was assigned a relative position within the participant's browsing sequence, ranging from 0 at the beginning to 1 at the end of the sequence. Posts were also classified according to the level of social reinforcement (high vs. low numbers of likes and comments). To capture changes between successive exposures, a binary variable indicated whether the thematic content category of the current post differed from that of the preceding post. Because no preceding post was available for the first observation, first posts were represented by a separate indicator rather than being classified as either changed or unchanged. Most posts contained a single image, although some contained multiple images. Multi-image posts were retained as single post-viewing episodes in the primary analyses, with characteristics taken from the first image displayed. Post type (single-vs. multiple-image) was included as a control variable.

Contextual characteristics

The platform automatically recorded the device used to access Travelgram, browser, time of day, and the location within the platform from which each post was viewed (main feed, explore page, or profile page). Most participants accessed Travelgram using a mobile device (67%), followed by desktop computers (31%) and tablets (2%). Chrome (61%) and Safari (14%) were the most commonly used browsers.

Person-level characteristics

Age and gender were assessed in the pre-use questionnaire. Impulsivity was measured using the eight-item Barratt Impulsiveness Scale-Brief [58], with responses ranging from 1 (rarely/never) to 4 (almost always/always). Item 8 ("I act on the spur of the moment.") showed a comparatively weak loading in the full eight-item model and was excluded. A two-factor model of the remaining seven items, representing Self-Control and Impulsive Action, fit the data well (χ 2 (13) = 76.95, p < .001, CFI = .995, TLI = .992, RMSEA = .067, SRMR = .042). The two factors were substantially correlated (r = .70). Because the present analyses concerned overall impulsivity rather than the sub-dimensions separately, the seven retained items were averaged to form a single composite score. Internal consistency was high (ω = .89; M = 1.72, SD = 0.58).

Interest in travel was assessed using six self-developed items capturing general interest in travel (e.g., "I enjoy exploring new places or cultures") and engagement with travel-related social media content (e.g., "When I travel, I often post photos or stories on social media"). Responses ranged from 1 (strongly disagree) to 5 (strongly agree). A two-factor model fit the data well (χ 2 (8) = 21.54, p = .006, CFI = .999, TLI = .999, RMSEA = .039, SRMR = .020), and the factors were strongly correlated (r = .79). The six items were therefore averaged to form the overall travel-interest measure used in the analyses. Internal consistency was high (ω = .92; M = 3.97, SD = 0.91).

Dwell time

The primary outcome was dwell time, defined as the duration of a post-viewing episode. Travelgram generated timestamped telemetry when posts were viewed and when participants navigated between posts or platform locations. A viewing episode began with the first recorded view of a post and ended when the logs indicated that a different post was viewed or that the participant navigated elsewhere on the platform. Dwell time was calculated as the difference between these timestamps in seconds [4].

Consecutive actions relating to the same post, such as liking, saving, or clicking within it, did not initiate new episodes. For posts containing multiple images, the available telemetry did not support unambiguous allocation of elapsed time to each individual image. These posts were therefore treated as single post-viewing episodes, with the characteristics of the first displayed image used in the primary analyses. Dwell time consequently represents the duration for which a post was behaviorally presented during browsing. Longer dwell times provide greater opportunity for perceptual and cognitive processing, but do not establish that such processing occurred throughout the exposure.

Analysis approach

We first processed the timestamped behavioral logs to reconstruct continuous Travelgram sessions and discrete post-viewing episodes. We used platform-profile registration events to identify platform-use blocks. If multiple registration blocks were available for the same participant (i.e., they loaded the platform twice in quick succession), we retained the block containing the greatest amount of recorded platform activity. Sessions were bounded by the recorded return to the survey where available and were truncated at the first inactivity gap exceeding five minutes. Navigation events were then used to reconstruct participants' location within Travelgram and the sequence in which posts were encountered.

A post-viewing episode began when a post was viewed or selected and ended at the first subsequent event indicating the presentation of a different post or navigation to another platform location. This procedure yielded 45,630 complete post episodes. We then excluded 322 episodes with dwell times below 0.01 seconds, which were treated as falling below the minimum meaningful logging resolution. Participants contributing fewer than ten remaining study-post episodes were subsequently excluded. The resulting behavioral dataset comprised 43,921 episodes from 1,102 participants.

Episodes between 0.01 and 0.10 seconds were retained in the primary analyses. Such very brief exposures are plausible during rapid scrolling and could not be distinguished from genuine behavior on the basis of the telemetry alone. They accounted for approximately 21% of the final behavioral observations. Because dwell times were strongly positively skewed, the outcome was natural-log transformed for the multilevel models. Descriptive statistics and figures are presented in seconds wherever possible.

Associations with dwell time were estimated using linear mixed-effects models. The primary model included random intercepts for participant, post, and participant-by-post pair. The first two terms account for repeated observations from the same participant and repeated presentation of the same posts across participants, while the participant-by-post term accounts for repeated exposure by a participant to the same post. Approximately 32% of observed participant-post pairs occurred more than once.

The fixed effects included visual complexity, valence, arousal, face presence, thematic image content, experimentally manipulated social reinforcement, change in thematic content from the previous post, relative position within the browsing sequence, platform location, device type, post type, age, gender, impulsivity, and travel interest. The experimental face-prevalence condition (5%, 25%, or 90%) was additionally included to account for the parent-study manipulation. Face presence and social reinforcement were entered with an interaction to test whether reinforcement was associated with dwell time specifically for posts depicting faces. A separate indicator identified the first post in a sequence because content change could not be defined for that observation.

Continuous image characteristics and person-level characteristics were centered at their sample means. Relative sequence position was centered at 0.5, such that zero represented the midpoint of the browsing sequence. Categorical predictors were entered as factors. For predictors with more than two levels, we used omnibus tests to evaluate the factor as a whole rather than interpreting individual dummy coefficients in the absence of an overall association. Coefficients from the log-dwell models were exponentiated for interpretation as dwell-time ratios. Values above 1 indicate relatively longer dwell times and values below 1 relatively shorter dwell times.

To address RQ3, we fitted separate models for impulsivity, travel interest, and participant gender. Each model added interactions between the moderator and the post characteristics considered in the corresponding research question, including visual complexity, valence, arousal, face presence, image content, content change, and social reinforcement. These models were fitted using maximum likelihood and compared with corresponding models without the interaction block using likelihood-ratio tests. Gender moderation analyses were restricted to participants identifying as female or male because only one participant selected another gender category.

Gender congruence was assessed in a separate model restricted to posts depicting a female-or male-presenting person and participants identifying as female or male. Episodes were classified according to whether the depicted and participant gender were the same or different, and log dwell time was regressed on this indicator using the same random-intercept structure.

We used three sensitivity analyses to assess whether the primary findings depended on key processing decisions. First, the primary model was repeated after excluding episodes shorter than 0.10 seconds. Second, first posts were excluded to determine whether associations with progression through the browsing sequence were driven by initial exposure. Third, the model was restricted to single-image posts so that post-level image characteristics corresponded unambiguously to the entire displayed post.

Results

Descriptive patterns in dwell time

Dwell times were strongly right-skewed: the median viewing duration was 0.93 seconds, whereas the mean was 3.20 seconds (SD = 8.22). Approximately 20.7% of episodes lasted between 0.01 and 0.10 seconds, indicating that very brief exposures were common during browsing. Figure 2 shows the distribution of dwell times, variation between participants, and descriptive differences across devices and platform locations. Additional descriptive plots showing variation in dwell time across participant and post characteristics are provided in Figures S1 and S2 in the supplementary materials. Before adding the fixed effects, we evaluated the distribution of variance in log-transformed dwell time using a null model with random intercepts for participant, post, and participant-post pair. Participant differences accounted for 40.0% of the variance, while repeated exposure to a particular participant-post combination accounted for a further 5.2%. Variation attributable to posts themselves was comparatively small (0.1%), with the remaining 54.7% occurring between viewing episodes within these clusters. These estimates indicate substantial and relatively stable differences between participants, alongside considerable episode-to-episode variability.

Post characteristics and social reinforcement

Fixed effects accounted for 4.1% of the variance in log dwell time, while the full model, including the random effects, accounted for 46.9%. For RQ1, there was little evidence that the measured visual and affective characteristics of posts were associated with dwell time after accounting for the other predictors in the model. Visual complexity showed a small positive association that was not statistically significant (dwell-time ratio = 1.025, 95% CI [0.994, 1.056], p = .109). Valence (ratio = 0.995, 95% CI [0.973, 1.017], p = .626) and arousal (ratio = 1.004, 95% CI [0.986, 1.023], p = .661) were likewise not associated with dwell time. Thematic image content was not associated with dwell time overall, F (12, 165) = 1.21, p = .278. Face-present and face-absent posts did not differ in dwell time under either social-reinforcement condition. In the few-likes condition, face-present posts had similar dwell times to face-absent posts (dwell-time ratio = 1.022, 95% CI [0.949, 1.101], p = .569). The same was true in the many-likes condition (ratio = 0.998, 95% CI [0.928, 1.074], p = .959). Accordingly, for RQ2, we found no evidence that the experimentally manipulated level of social reinforcement altered the association between face presence and dwell time. The face-presence by reinforcement interaction was not significant (b = -0.024, SE = 0.037, p = .530).

Moderation by individual characteristics

For RQ3, we tested whether associations between post characteristics and dwell time differed as a function of impulsivity, travel interest, or participant gender. Adding the corresponding interaction blocks did not improve model fit for impulsivity, χ 2 (18) = 17.62, p = .481, travel interest, χ 2 (18) = 15.83, p = .604, or participant gender, χ 2 (18) = 17.71, p = .475. We therefore found no evidence that the associations between the measured post characteristics and dwell time were systematically moderated by these individual characteristics.

Content change and progression through the browsing sequence

For RQ4, changing thematic content from one study post to the next was not associated with dwell time. Posts whose content category differed from the preceding post had similar dwell times to posts whose content category remained the same (dwell-time ratio = 0.980, 95% CI [0.948, 1.015], p = .257).

For RQ5, dwell time declined substantially as participants progressed through the browsing sequence. Moving from the beginning to the end of the sequence was associated with a dwell-time ratio of 0.475 (95% CI [0.454, 0.497], p < .001), corresponding to approximately 52.5% shorter dwell times at the end relative to the beginning of the sequence, holding the other variables in the model constant. First posts were also viewed substantially longer than subsequent posts (b = 1.218, p < .001), and this first-post difference was modelled separately from the continuous sequence-progression effect. Figure 3 illustrates the descriptive decline in dwell time across deciles of relative position within the browsing sequence. Note. Viewing episodes were divided into deciles according to their relative position within each participant's browsing sequence, from early (1) to late (10). For each participant, median dwell time was calculated within each decile; points show the median of these participant-level medians and the shaded region shows 95% confidence intervals obtained by bootstrapping participants. Dwell time is shown on a logarithmic scale.

Viewing context

For RQ6, dwell time differed substantially according to where posts were viewed within the platform, F (2, 42467) = 97.92, p < .001. Relative to posts viewed in the main feed, dwell times were longer when posts were viewed from profile pages (dwell-time ratio = 1.790, 95% CI [1.520, 2.109], p < .001) and especially from the explore page (ratio = 2.864, 95% CI [2.425, 3.383], p < .001). Thus, after adjustment for the other predictors in the model, posts viewed from profiles were associated with approximately 1.8 times the dwell time observed in the main feed, while posts viewed from the explore page were associated with approximately 2.9 times the dwell time. By contrast, there was no overall association between device type and dwell time, F (2, 1099) = 2.19, p = .112. Relative to desktop use, the estimated dwell-time ratios were 0.883 for mobile devices (95% CI [0.749, 1.042]) and 0.655 for tablets (95% CI [0.408, 1.053]).

Gender congruence

For RQ7, we assessed whether participants dwelled longer on posts depicting individuals of a different gender than their own. The analysis included 21,825 viewing episodes from 1,088 participants and 100 posts depicting a female-or male-presenting person. Dwell time did not differ between posts depicting someone of the same versus a different gender (dwell-time ratio = 0.995, 95% CI [0.950, 1.041], p = .819). We therefore found no evidence that gender congruence was associated with viewing duration.

Findings summary and sensitivity analyses

Figure 4 summarizes the focal estimates across all of the research questions. The clearest associations were the decline in dwell time across the browsing sequence and the longer dwell times observed when posts were viewed from profile and explore pages rather than the main feed. By comparison, most measured post characteristics, social reinforcement, and individual characteristics showed small or imprecisely estimated associations with dwell time. Sensitivity analyses indicated that the main pattern of results was largely unchanged when first posts were excluded and when analyses were restricted to single-image posts. In particular, the association with progression through the browsing sequence was virtually unchanged after excluding first posts (dwell-time ratio = 0.476, 95% CI [0.455, 0.498], compared with 0.475 in the primary model) and remained similar when restricting the analysis to single-image posts (ratio = 0.488, 95% CI [0.466, 0.512]). Estimates for the other focal predictors were also generally similar under these two specifications.

Excluding episodes shorter than 0.10 seconds produced somewhat larger differences. The decline across the browsing sequence remained evident but was attenuated (ratio = 0.710, 95% CI [0.680, 0.742]), as were the associations with viewing posts from profile pages (ratio = 1.301, 95% CI [1.128, 1.499]) and the explore page (ratio = 2.128, 95% CI [1.845, 2.454]). In this restricted sample, mobile (ratio = 0.820, 95% CI [0.732, 0.918]) and tablet viewing (ratio = 0.686, 95% CI [0.496, 0.950]) were associated with shorter dwell times relative to desktop viewing, and visual complexity showed a small positive association with dwell time (ratio = 1.037, 95% CI [1.008, 1.067]). Estimates for the remaining post-and individual-level predictors were broadly similar to those from the primary model.

Discussion

We investigated how long users dwelled on individual posts while browsing a simulated image-based social media platform. This is a basic but consequential feature of social media use because the duration of an exposure constrains the opportunity users have to perceive and process the content they encounter. Aggregate measures of platform use, or even records of which posts appeared on screen, therefore provide an incomplete perspective on exposure if users move past some posts almost immediately while dwelling much longer on others. Across more than 43,000 post-viewing episodes, we found that exposure was typically brief, with the median dwell time lasting less than a second. At the same time, dwell time varied considerably both within and between participants. The clearest systematic associations were not with the measured visual or affective characteristics of individual posts, but with where participants were in their browsing sequence and where within the platform a post was encountered. Social reinforcement, participant characteristics, and gender congruence showed little evidence of association with dwell time.

These findings extend previous studies showing substantial variation in the duration of social media exposures [14] [15] [16] [17]. Prior work has reported viewing durations ranging from fractions of a second to several seconds or more, depending on the platform, content, and measurement approach. Our results add evidence from an interactive environment in which viewing duration emerged from participants' own scrolling and navigation rather than from a predefined sequence or researcher-controlled presentation. More generally, they contribute to efforts to strengthen the descriptive foundations of research on digital media use by documenting a basic feature of behavior that is otherwise difficult for independent researchers to observe [19] [20] [21].

Brief and heterogeneous exposure during feed browsing

The observed distribution of dwell times provides an empirical reference point for research concerned with exposure to social media content. Many encounters were extremely brief, while a smaller subset involved substantially longer periods on screen. This is consistent with earlier work using screen recording, eye-tracking, and simulated feeds [14] [15] [16] [17]. Anderson [16] reported dwell times ranging from under a second to over 20 seconds in a simulated Twitter feed, and Ellison et al. [14] found that Facebook users viewed posts for 7-8 seconds on average.

Although dwell time should not be equated with visual attention or cognitive processing [59], it defines the period during which such processing can occur [4]. A post visible for several seconds affords considerably greater opportunity for perception, appraisal, and encoding than one passed within a fraction of a second. The brevity of many exposures, therefore, has implications for experimental studies of social media content. Many studies necessarily present posts as isolated or sequential stimuli for researcher-determined periods, whereas everyday feed browsing is user paced and often considerably more rapid. Such designs can be appropriate when sustained exposure is required to test a particular mechanism, but they represent a different exposure condition from the rapid scrolling typical of contemporary social media use. Our findings reinforce the value of distinguishing what a message can do under controlled exposure from how long similar content is ordinarily available for processing during browsing. Researchers should therefore distinguish between effects demonstrated under experimentally sustained exposure and the exposure durations that arise during user-controlled browsing

The results also illustrate some of the heterogeneity obscured by broad descriptions of "passive" social media use. Browsing is commonly distinguished from active behaviors like posting or commenting [5, 6], although this distinction has increasingly been questioned [7]. The present behavioral data show that even within browsing, superficially similar periods of use can involve rapid transitions across many posts, longer pauses on selected content, movement between platform locations, and repeated exposures. Aggregate measures of time spent browsing therefore provide limited information about the exposure events from which that time is composed [60].

The prevalence of very brief exposures does not necessarily mean that these encounters were perceptually empty. Research on active vision shows that people can acquire task-relevant visual information rapidly and selectively rather than encoding every encountered object in detail [22, 23]. Rapid scrolling may similarly involve brief samples that provide enough information to support the decision to continue or move on.

Dwell time changes across the browsing sequence

The strongest temporal pattern was a marked decline in dwell time as browsing progressed. Holding the other predictors constant, estimated dwell time at the end of the browsing sequence was approximately half that at the beginning. First posts were viewed especially long, but excluding them produced an almost identical estimate for sequence progression, indicating that the broader decline was not simply an artefact of unusually long initial exposures. This result is consistent with previous evidence that viewing behaviour changes over the course of social media browsing. Epstein and Lin [47], for example, similarly observed declining dwell time within a simulated social media session, while other work has provided evidence of the importance of temporal position, adaptation, and continuity between successive media encounters [15] [16] [17] 38].

Several mechanisms could produce this decline. Participants may become familiar with the interface and adopt a faster scrolling rhythm, become increasingly selective, or lose interest in the available content as the session continues. Adaptation or fatigue are also possible explanations [61]. The present data cannot distinguish between these mechanisms, however, because position in the browsing sequence necessarily covaries with elapsed time and accumulated exposure. The finding nevertheless shows that exposure duration is temporally structured within a browsing session. A post encountered early and the same post encountered later need not receive equivalent exposure, even when its observable characteristics are unchanged. Studies of feed-based media use, or content exposure, may consequently benefit from treating position within a usage session as part of the exposure context rather than assuming equivalent exposure throughout browsing.

Limited explanatory power of measured post characteristics

A second notable finding was the limited explanatory power of the measured characteristics of individual posts. Visual complexity, valence, arousal, face presence, thematic content, and changes in content from the preceding post showed little evidence of association with dwell time in the primary model. Experimentally manipulated social reinforcement likewise did not reliably extend viewing duration.

These null associations are informative in light of research showing that visual characteristics can shape perceptual selection and gaze. Faces, contrast, complexity, and affective properties have all been associated with visual attention in other contexts [27] [28] [29] [30] [31] [32] [33]. Our findings do not contradict this work. Rather, they suggest that attracting gaze to a particular element of an image and increasing the total time a user remains on a post are distinct outcomes. A face may influence where someone looks without substantially delaying the decision to continue scrolling.

A similar distinction may help interpret the social-reinforcement result. Likes and related metrics can communicate popularity or social endorsement [34, 35], but evidence that they influence viewing duration has been mixed. Anderson [16] likewise reported little evidence that visible engagement cues affected dwell time, and Haim et al. [34] found limited effects of popularity cues on attention. In the present study, increasing social reinforcement did not reliably increase dwell time for posts depicting faces.

We similarly found little evidence that the associations between post characteristics and dwell time differed systematically by impulsivity, travel interest, or participant gender. Nor did participants spend longer on posts depicting people of a different gender, despite previous studies reporting gender-related differences in visual attention to depicted individuals [44, 45].

The limited associations with visual complexity, faces, and affective characteristics may also reflect the difference between viewing static images and acting within an ongoing visual task. Research on natural vision shows that gaze can be shaped more strongly by current goals and behaviour than by intrinsic visual salience [62]. Feed browsing similarly embeds individual posts within a continuing sequence of decisions. Features that influence where users look within an image may therefore have little effect on how long they remain on the post.

Browsing context matters

Platform location was one of the strongest correlates of dwell time. Relative to posts encountered in the main feed, dwell times were approximately 1.8 times longer on profile pages and 2.9 times longer on the explore page. This is consistent with broader evidence that the context and interface through which content is encountered can shape media use [39]. It also supports treating exposure as more than a property of the message itself. The same type of content may be encountered differently depending on how the user arrived at it. Opening a post from a set of thumbnails or navigating to a profile may identify content in which a user was already interested, while differences in interface structure may independently alter the mechanics of browsing. The observed location effects likely reflect some combination of selection and interface context.

Device differences were less consistent. Device type was not associated with dwell time overall in the primary model, although mobile and tablet viewing were associated with shorter dwell times once episodes below 0.10 seconds were excluded. Previous work has similarly shown that device characteristics can alter scrolling and information processing [25, 26, 40, 41], although Mayer et al. [15] observed slightly longer viewing durations on smartphones than desktops. The differences across studies suggest that device effects may depend on the interface, exposure content, measurement approach, and treatment of extremely brief exposures rather than reflecting a simple general difference between mobile and desktop use.

Data-cleaning decisions should be made explicit

The sensitivity analysis excluding episodes shorter than 0.10 seconds provides an additional methodological insight. Removing these observations attenuated the association with sequence progression and reduced the differences between the main feed and profile and explore pages. Importantly, there was no empirical basis for distinguishing logging error from genuine rapid transitions within this range. Treating them all as invalid would therefore remove a substantial portion of the behaviour that characterises rapid scrolling. More generally, digital trace data do not arrive as self-evident measures of behaviour. Researchers must make consequential decisions about how records are cleaned, reconstructed, excluded, and translated into analytic events [8, 63]. Researchers should therefore make these decisions explicit and evaluate whether substantive conclusions depend on them.

Limitations and directions for future research

Several limitations qualify these findings. First, although the simulated environment provided high realism, it was still a simulated platform. Its content was restricted to travel-related static images, did not include video or algorithmic personalization, and was not drawn from participants' own social networks. These design choices provided experimental control and made post-viewing duration largely dependent on participants' own navigation, but they also limit generalizability to platforms where content is more personally relevant, emotionally varied, or adaptively ranked. Participants also browsed for a relatively short, researcher-defined period, and their goals may have differed from those governing everyday social media use.

Second, dwell time measures presentation duration rather than visual attention. A post remaining on screen does not establish that the user was looking at it, and a very brief exposure does not establish that nothing was perceived or processed. Likewise, longer dwell time provides more opportunity for processing but does not indicate what was attended to within the post. Combining platform telemetry with eye-tracking, screen recording, or other measures of momentary behavior would allow future research to distinguish presentation, visual attention, and subsequent processing more directly.

Third, several predictors were observational even though the parent study experimentally manipulated face prevalence and social reinforcement. Associations with sequence position, platform location, device, and coded image characteristics should therefore not be given causal interpretations. Future work could experimentally manipulate specific post characteristics, navigation structures, or feed-ranking rules while retaining user-controlled browsing to identify which aspects of the environment causally alter exposure duration.

Finally, the study concerned one platform design and one adult UK sample. Replication across content domains, populations, interfaces, and naturalistic browsing environments is needed to establish which patterns generalise. In particular, combining controlled simulated-platform studies with data donation or in-the-wild instrumentation could test whether the brief exposure durations, large between-person differences, and decline across browsing sequences observed here also characterize everyday platform use [64].

Conclusion

This study provides a high-resolution perspective on dwell time during user-controlled browsing of an image-based social media platform. Consistent with prior work, post exposures were typically brief and strongly skewed. More importantly, dwell time varied systematically across the browsing sequence and between platform locations, whereas the measured post and participant characteristics accounted for comparatively little variation within this controlled stimulus set. In this setting, when and where content was encountered were therefore more strongly associated with exposure duration than the measured characteristics of the content or viewer.

The paper draws attention to exposure duration as an important but distinct component of social media use. Knowing that a post appeared in a feed, or that a user spent a given amount of time on a platform, provides limited information about how long individual pieces of content were actually available for processing. Simulated platforms offer one way to study this intermediate level of behavior transparently and at high temporal resolution, particularly for behavioral signals that are difficult for independent researchers to access on commercial platforms. At the same time, such logs capture exposure rather than visual attention or cognitive processing. Future work combining simulated-platform telemetry with theory-driven manipulations and complementary measures such as eye-tracking or psychophysiological indicators can help establish when brief encounters with social media content matter and why.
